questions.q: According to this lesson's research, does Snowflake document a single feature literally named "human-in-the-loop" that covers every Cortex Agent tool type?
options: No — it documents a specific permission_policy mechanism for the code execution tool, and a broader pattern (Agent Identity + Horizon policies + your own approval step) for other tool types
Yes — every tool type ships an identical, named human-in-the-loop feature
No — Snowflake has no approval mechanism anywhere in Cortex Agents
Yes, but only for Cortex Search, never for code execution
questions.explain: This lesson is explicit that Snowflake's documented mechanism is scoped to the code execution tool's permission_policy; other tool types require assembling the equivalent pattern from Agent Identity, Horizon policies, and an application-layer gate.

questions.q: Where does permission_policy live in a Cortex Agent's configuration?
options: Nested under tool_resources, under the specific tool's name (e.g. code_execution)
As a top-level account parameter set via ALTER ACCOUNT
Inside the ground-truth evaluation dataset
In the CLASSIFICATION_PROFILE object
questions.explain: The permission_policy field nests under tool_resources, under the relevant tool's name, such as code_execution.

questions.q: What is the default permission_policy value, and what does it do?
options: always_ask — it always prompts for approval before executing a state-modifying tool call
always_allow — it executes everything without asking, by default
never_ask — it never requires approval under any configuration
manual_only — it requires a human to type every tool call by hand
questions.explain: always_ask is the default, and it prompts for approval before any state-modifying tool call executes.

questions.q: Under always_ask, what actually happens when the agent reaches a state-modifying call?
options: It emits a tool_use event and stops execution entirely, resuming only after the caller sends a permission_decision referencing that tool call
It executes the call immediately and logs it for later review
It silently skips the call and moves to the next step
It retries the call up to three times before giving up
questions.explain: The agent genuinely pauses — emitting a tool_use event and waiting for a permission_decision content block before resuming, not just flagging the action after it already ran.

questions.q: For a tool type like Cortex Analyst or Cortex Search, which doesn't ship a documented permission_policy, what does this lesson recommend assembling instead?
options: Agent Identity (to know an agent is acting) + a Horizon row access/masking policy as a backstop + your own application-layer approval gate
Nothing — these tool types cannot be governed at all
A CLASSIFICATION_PROFILE applied to the agent's own user account
Disabling the tool entirely, since no governance is possible
questions.explain: The lesson teaches building the equivalent pattern yourself: Agent Identity for detection, a Horizon policy as a hard backstop, and an application-layer gate implementing the same pause-and-wait shape.
